problem: Static geometric maps and reactive planners only avoid hazards that are visible or already experienced; prior semantic or risk-aware methods (e.g. E2Map) update costs only after a harmful event, so latent dynamic hazards such as a door that may open are not handled proactively.
motivation: Robots in human-centric or hazardous settings must anticipate dangers before they materialize, as humans do through inference and anxiety-like caution. VLMs hold broad prior knowledge about risky situations, so their reasoning can be turned into navigation cost without trial-and-error experience.
key_idea: Use a VLM to reason about potential hazards in the scene, score each with an anxiety value, segment the hazards zero-shot, and project them as Gaussian-propagated costs fused with a geometric obstacle map for planning.
insight: Language-derived a-priori risk lets the robot avoid latent hazards (a closed door, a seated person on a chair) with no prior collision. In simulation, the reactive geometric map fails 0/10 on both latent-hazard scenarios, and E2Map, which updates only after events, reaches 9/10 while the proposed method reaches 10/10. The authors frame the approach as a-priori and E2Map as a-posteriori, and suggest combining them. They note a safety-versus-efficiency trade-off, with slightly longer paths when no hazard is present.
method: Hazard Reasoner: GPT-4o takes the RGB image and a prompt and outputs JSON with a scene description, object list, chain-of-thought hazard reasoning and a list of hazardous objects.

Emotion Evaluator: GPT-4o-mini takes the reasoning, hazardous objects and image and assigns each object an anxiety score from 1 to 3 with CoT justification (adapted from E2Map). Each VLM cycle takes about 4 s.

Language-based segmentation: Grounded Edge SAM segments the hazardous objects named by the VLM in each new frame, running faster than the VLM using the latest hazard list, with masks labeled by anxiety score.
Anxiety score map: masks are merged with depth into a 3D point cloud, filtered, and projected onto the 2D grid, giving cell scores in {0,1,2,3}.

Gaussian cost propagation: each hazard cell spreads cost with a 2D Gaussian whose std is scaled by log(a/T), following the Weber-Fechner law, with amplitude a/3 clamped to [0,1] and max over overlapping hazards.
Map fusion: M_Gaussian = max(obstacle map, cost map) in [0,1], fed to D* Lite planning and MPPI control, updated incrementally during navigation.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (hazard reasoner, frozen) + GPT-4o-mini (emotion evaluator, frozen) + Grounded Edge SAM (zero-shot segmentation)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (ZED stereo camera in real-world data), plus pose from simulator or VINS-Mono
setting.action_space: planned paths via D* Lite on a cost grid, executed by MPPI velocity control on a quadruped
setting.simulator: Gazebo (Unitree Go1); real-world data recorded offline with Earth Rover Zero
setting.privileged: localization taken directly from the simulator in Gazebo experiments; otherwise none

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 runs (forward and reverse routes) in a custom Gazebo room

numbers_note: Only a small custom Gazebo evaluation (three scenarios, 10 runs each). Real-world results are qualitative map visualizations on offline data, with no metrics.
results: In three Gazebo hazard scenarios the method succeeded 10/10 on each. The geometric map got 10/10, 0/10 and 0/10, and E2Map, the strongest baseline, got 9/10 on each scenario. Real-world offline data qualitatively show raised costs around doors, seated people, elevators and snow.
limitations: Evaluation is tiny and custom (three scenarios, 10 runs each) with no standard benchmark, and real-world results are offline and qualitative only.
VLM inference takes about 4 s per cycle and depends on proprietary GPT-4o models, limiting reactivity; the method may lengthen paths when no hazards are present.
